mainTopic: Humility, reward and punishment, the limits of יום הכפורים, and appeasing someone you have hurt
overview: This amud opens with how great leaders kept themselves humble: רב when he went out to judge, and רב זוטרא while he was carried in honor. The גמרא then explains the verse 'שאת פני רשע לא טוב'. It is bad for the wicked, like אחאב, to be spared in this world, and good for the righteous, like משה, to be punished here. The merit of צדיקים protects their descendants, while the guilt of רשעים harms theirs. One who brings the public to merit is protected from sin, but one who leads the public to sin can almost never do תשובה. Returning to the משנה, the גמרא explains why 'אחטא ואשוב' is said twice: a repeated sin comes to feel permitted. It also shows that even רבי agrees יום הכפורים does not atone for someone who sinned while relying on it. Sins against another person need the victim to be appeased, and the amud gives the rules: even for words, up to three times, and at the grave if he has died. Stories about רבי ירמיה, רבי זירא and רב show this in practice, and a new story about רב reading before רבי begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב's humble words when going out to judge
steps.stepSummary: רב reminds himself that public leadership is dangerous. He gains nothing for his family from it, and he can only hope to come home as free of sin as he left.
steps.simpleTranslation: Of his own will he goes out to die. He does not take care of his household's needs, and he goes back home empty-handed. If only his coming home would be like his going out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting what רב would say to himself each time he went out to serve as a judge (the opening of the quote is on the previous amud).
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treats judging as a life-and-death risk, because a wrong ruling carries heavy punishment. He takes no personal profit from the job. His only wish is to return home without having sinned, just as he left.

keyTerms.meaning: the coming in should be like the going out (return without sin)

steps.confusionAlert: The speaker here is רב. This amud starts in the middle of his statement, which was introduced on the previous lines.

phrases.english: Of his own will he goes out to death,
phrases.notes: Judging carries the risk of punishment for a wrong ruling.

phrases.english: and he does not do the will (needs) of his household,
and he goes back to his house empty-handed,
and if only the coming in would be like the going out.
phrases.notes: He hopes to return as free of sin as when he left.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the quote of רב on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A leader or judge should view his role as a dangerous burden, not as personal gain.

steps.title: רב quotes איוב when a crowd follows him
steps.stepSummary: When רב saw a crowd following him in his honor, he quoted a verse from איוב. The verse says that even someone raised to the heavens can disappear completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he saw a crowd behind him, he would say: 'Even if his greatness rises to the heavens and his head reaches the clouds, he will be lost forever like his own dung. Those who saw him will say: Where is he?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another humbling habit of רב: when people honored him by following him, he recited a verse about how quickly greatness disappears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Public honor can lead to arrogance. רב fought that feeling by reminding himself that even the highest person can vanish completely. The image is harsh on purpose: it breaks pride.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי הָוֵי חָזֵי אַמְבּוּהָא אַבָּתְרֵיהּ, אָמַר:
phrases.english: And when he would see a crowd behind him, he said:
"Though his greatness rises to the heavens,
and his head reaches the clouds,
like his own dung he will perish forever;
those who saw him will say: Where is he?"
phrases.notes: איוב כ:ו-ז

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second humility practice of the same רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When honored publicly, a leader should remind himself how temporary greatness is.

steps.title: רב זוטרא's verse while being carried in honor
steps.stepSummary: רב זוטרא was carried on people's shoulders on the festival שבת. While being carried, he recited a verse saying that power does not last forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they would carry רב זוטרא on their shoulders on the שבת of the festival, he would say: 'For power is not forever, nor does the crown last for all generations.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a parallel example from רב זוטרא, who also guarded himself against pride during a moment of great honor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the festival שבת, when big crowds gathered for the public lecture, people would carry the lecturer to honor him. רב זוטרא used a verse from משלי to remind himself that this honor is temporary.

keyTerms.meaning: the שבת of the festival (when a public lecture was given)

steps.whatToRemember: Great leaders (רב, רב זוטרא) actively fought pride by reciting verses about how temporary honor and power are.

phrases.aramaic: רַב זוּטְרָא, כִּי הֲווֹ מְכַתְּפִי לֵיהּ
phrases.english: Rav Zutra, when they would carry him on their shoulders
on the Shabbos of the festival, would say:
"For power is not forever,
and does the crown last for every generation?"
phrases.notes: משלי כז:כד

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב זוּטְרָא, כִּי הֲווֹ מְכַתְּפִי לֵיהּ בְּשַׁבְּתָא דְרִיגְלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel example from a different אמורא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even at the height of honor, one should remember that power is temporary.

steps.title: It is bad for the wicked to be favored in this world: אחאב
steps.stepSummary: The verse 'שאת פני רשע לא טוב' is read to mean that it is bad for the wicked to be spared punishment in this world. אחאב is the example.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Showing favor to the wicked is not good.' It is not good for the wicked that they are shown favor in this world. It was not good for אחאב that he was shown favor in this world, as it says: 'Because אחאב humbled himself before Me, I will not bring the evil in his days.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new teaching. It explains a verse to mean that being spared in this world is actually bad for a wicked person, and proves it from אחאב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a wicked person does a little good, ה׳ may reward him in this world by delaying his punishment. That leaves him with nothing in עולם הבא. אחאב humbled himself, so his punishment was pushed off to after his lifetime. His reward was 'used up' here.

keyTerms.meaning: showing favor / going easy on someone
אחאב, the wicked king of Israel

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'favor' does not mean a true blessing. Being spared now is described as bad, because the wicked person gets paid off in this world instead of the next.

phrases.english: "Showing favor to the wicked is not good" —
phrases.notes: משלי יח:ה

phrases.english: it is not good for the wicked
that they are shown favor in this world.
It was not good for Achav
that he was shown favor in this world,
as it is said: "Because he (Achav) humbled himself before Me,
I will not bring the evil in his days."
phrases.notes: מלכים א כא:כט

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new aggadic teaching on a related theme of honor and favor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being spared punishment in this world is bad for the wicked; אחאב is the proof.

steps.title: It is good for the righteous not to be favored in this world: משה
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the verse teaches the opposite. It is good for צדיקים to be punished in this world, and משה is the example. Had he not sinned, he would not yet have died.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'To turn aside the righteous in judgment' means it is good for the righteous that they are not shown favor in this world. It was good for משה that he was not shown favor in this world, as it says: 'Because you did not believe in Me, to sanctify Me.' This implies that had you believed in Me, your time to leave the world would not yet have come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the second half of the same verse as the mirror image. Being judged strictly in this world is good for a צדיק, and משה proves it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה was punished right away in this world for the episode of the rock, and died before entering ארץ ישראל. The words 'because you did not believe' show that his death at that time came from the sin itself. So he paid for it here and kept his full reward for עולם הבא.

keyTerms.meaning: to turn aside / to judge strictly
to depart from the world (to die)

steps.whyThisMatters: Together with step 4, this sets out a key principle of reward and punishment. The wicked are paid in this world for their few merits. The righteous pay in this world for their few sins.

phrases.english: "To turn aside the righteous in judgment" —
it is good for the righteous

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין נוֹשְׂאִין לָהֶם פָּנִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
phrases.english: that they are not shown favor in this world.
It was good for Moshe

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא נָשְׂאוּ לוֹ פָּנִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
phrases.english: that he was not shown favor in this world,
as it is said: "Because you did not believe in Me, to sanctify Me,"
phrases.notes: במדבר כ:יב

phrases.english: implying: had you believed in Me —

phrases.aramaic: עֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ זְמַנָּם לִיפָּטֵר מִן הָעוֹלָם.
phrases.english: their time to depart the world would not yet have come.
phrases.notes: 'Their' refers to משה and אהרן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror image of step 4, taken from the second half of the same verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being judged strictly in this world benefits the righteous; משה died early for his sin, keeping his reward complete.

steps.title: The merit of the righteous protects their descendants
steps.stepSummary: Fortunate are the צדיקים: their merit helps not only themselves but also their children and grandchildren forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fortunate are the righteous! It is not enough that they earn merit for themselves; they also earn merit for their children and grandchildren until the end of all generations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a new praise of צדיקים. Their good deeds benefit their descendants for all time. A proof follows in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a new idea beyond reward for oneself: merit passes down to one's family. This sets up the example of אהרן's sons that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not enough for them

phrases.english: Fortunate are the righteous,
not only do they themselves earn merit,
but they bring merit to their children and their children's children
until the end of all generations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new praise of צדיקים, following the discussion of how they are treated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The merit of the righteous protects their descendants forever.

steps.title: Proof from אהרן's surviving sons
steps.stepSummary: אהרן's other sons deserved to be burned like נדב ואביהוא, as the word 'הנותרים' shows. They were saved only by their father's merit.
steps.simpleTranslation: For אהרן had several sons who deserved to be burned like נדב ואביהוא, as it says 'who were left'. But their father's merit protected them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the claim of step 6 using the verse about אהרן's sons who were 'left' after נדב ואביהוא died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'הנותרים' (those left) suggests that the surviving sons, אלעזר and איתמר, were also in line for the same punishment and only 'remained'. What saved them was אהרן's merit, which kept them and their descendants as כהנים forever.

keyTerms.meaning: נדב ואביהוא, אהרן's sons who died by fire

steps.whatToRemember: The wicked are paid in this world and lose the next. The righteous pay for their sins here and keep their full reward. Their merit even protects their children for all generations.

phrases.english: For Aharon had several sons
who deserved to be burned like Nadav and Avihu,
as it is said: "who were left,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא י:טז

phrases.english: but their father's merit stood up for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the proof for the claim made in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That the merit of צדיקים protects their descendants.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'הנותרים' in ויקרא י:טז, describing אהרן's surviving sons.

steps.title: Woe to the wicked: their guilt harms their descendants
steps.stepSummary: The opposite of the previous teaching: the guilt of רשעים harms their children and grandchildren forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: Woe to the wicked! It is not enough that they make themselves guilty. They also make their children and grandchildren guilty, until the end of all generations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other side of step 6. צדיקים help their descendants, and רשעים hurt theirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said a צדיק's merit protects his family for generations. This step says guilt works the same way: a רשע's sin can bring harm on his family for generations. The two statements are a matched pair.

phrases.english: Woe to the wicked,
it is not enough for them that they make themselves guilty,
but they also make their children and grandchildren guilty
until the end of all generations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirror image of the statement about צדיקים in step 6
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guilt of the wicked passes on to their descendants for all generations.

steps.title: כנען's children lost greatness because of their father
steps.stepSummary: Example: many of כנען's descendants were worthy of סמיכה like טבי, but their father's sin kept them as slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: כנען had many children who were worthy of being ordained as rabbis, like טבי, the servant of רבן גמליאל. But their father's guilt held them back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives an example to prove step 8. כנען was cursed to be a slave, and so his talented descendants stayed slaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טבי was a slave known for great wisdom, so slaves from כנען could be truly worthy of סמיכה. They could not receive it only because כנען's curse made them slaves. This shows a father's guilt affecting later generations.

keyTerms.meaning: son of חם, cursed to be a slave (בראשית ט)
the wise servant of רבן גמליאל

phrases.english: Canaan had many children
who were worthy of being ordained
like Tavi, the servant of Rabban Gamliel,
but their father's guilt caused it for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an example for the rule in step 8, matching how step 7 gave an example for step 6
steps.raayaObject: The guilt of the wicked harms their descendants
steps.raayaSupportSource: כנען's worthy descendants who stayed slaves

steps.title: Bringing the public to merit versus leading them to sin
steps.stepSummary: Whoever brings the many to merit is protected from sin. Whoever leads the many to sin can almost never do תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever brings merit to the public will not have a sin come about through him. Whoever causes the public to sin is almost never given the chance to do תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a new pair of rules. Influencing many people for good or for bad changes how Heaven treats the person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the theme of one person affecting others. A teacher's effect on his students works like a father's effect on his children. The reasons for both rules come in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: one who brings the public to merit (good deeds)
one who causes the public to sin
he is not given the chance

phrases.english: Whoever brings merit to the public —
sin will not come about through him,
and whoever causes the public to sin —
is almost not given the opportunity
to repent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching about influence, this time on students and the public
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bringing the public to merit protects a person from sin. Leading the public to sin almost blocks תשובה.

steps.title: Why is one who brings merit to the public protected from sin?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the first half of step 10.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever brings merit to the public will not have sin come about through him. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the first rule and asks why it is true. This sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule was stated without a reason. The גמרא wants to know why Heaven gives special protection to such a person.

phrases.english: Whoever brings merit to the public —
sin will not come about through him,
what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind step 10
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason one who brings merit to the many is protected from sin

steps.title: So the teacher will not be in גיהנם while his students are in גן עדן
steps.stepSummary: It would not be fitting for the teacher to end up in גיהנם while the students he brought to merit enjoy גן עדן.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that he will not be in גיהנם while his students are in גן עדן. As the verse says: 'For You will not leave my soul in the grave; You will not let Your devoted one see the pit.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Heaven protects him so he will not be punished while the people he helped are rewarded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It would be unfair for the source of others' merit to lose out himself. The פסוק in תהלים shows that ה׳ does not let His devoted one go down to the pit.

phrases.english: so that he will not be in Gehenna
while his students are in the Garden of Eden,
as it says: "For You will not abandon my soul to the netherworld;
You will not let Your devoted one see the pit."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: So he will not be in גיהנם while his students are in גן עדן (תהלים טז:י)

steps.title: So the sinner will not be in גן עדן while his students are in גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: One who leads others to sin is not helped to do תשובה. Otherwise he would be saved while his victims suffer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And whoever causes the public to sin is not given the chance to do תשובה. This is so that he will not be in גן עדן while his students are in גיהנם. As the verse says: 'A man weighed down with the blood of a person will flee to the pit; let no one support him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the matching reason for the second rule. It would be unfair for the one who caused the sin to be saved while his followers are punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror of step 12. The פסוק in משלי describes someone 'weighed down with blood,' meaning he spiritually destroyed others, and says no one will hold him back from the pit. That is why Heaven does not help him do תשובה.

keyTerms.meaning: weighed down with the blood of a person

steps.confusionAlert: Step 10 said 'almost' (כמעט) no chance to do תשובה. The door is not fully closed. It is only made very hard.

phrases.english: And whoever causes the public to sin —
is not given the opportunity to repent,
so that he will not be in the Garden of Eden
while his students are in Gehenna,
as it says: "A man weighed down with the blood of a person

phrases.aramaic: עַד בּוֹר יָנוּס אַל יִתְמְכוּ בוֹ״.
phrases.english: will flee to the pit; let none support him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel reasoning for the second half of step 10
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: So he will not be in גן עדן while his students are in גיהנם (משלי כח:יז)
steps.whatToRemember: Influence on others counts. Bringing others to good protects you from sin, and leading others to sin makes תשובה nearly impossible.

steps.title: Why does the משנה repeat 'I will sin and repent' twice?
steps.stepSummary: Back to the משנה: the גמרא asks why the phrase 'אחטא ואשוב' appears twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'One who says, I will sin and repent, I will sin and repent' is not given the chance to repent. Why does it need to say 'I will sin and repent' two times?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the words of the משנה and quotes them. It asks why the phrase is doubled, which sets up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One time seems to be enough to describe someone who plans to sin and then repent. The repetition must teach something, so the גמרא asks what that is.

keyTerms.meaning: I will sin and I will repent

phrases.english: One who says: I will sin and I will repent,
I will sin and I will repent.
Why do I need to say
"I will sin and repent, I will sin and repent"
two times?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadic material and goes back to the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for the doubled phrase in the משנה

steps.title: After repeating a sin, it becomes 'permitted' to him
steps.stepSummary: Following רב הונא in the name of רב: once a person repeats a sin, it becomes permitted to him. That is why the משנה says it twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows רב הונא in the name of רב. רב הונא said in the name of רב: once a person does a sin and repeats it, it becomes permitted to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the double wording teaches about repeating a sin. After the second time, the sin feels permitted, so תשובה becomes very hard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first 'I will sin and repent' is one sin. The second is the repetition, and after it the person is stuck. That explains why the משנה says he is not given the chance to repent.

phrases.english: In accordance with what Rav Huna said in the name of Rav.
For Rav Huna said in the name of Rav:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁעָבַר אָדָם עֲבֵירָה וְשָׁנָה בָּהּ —
phrases.english: Once a person commits a sin and repeats it —
it becomes permitted to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The repetition shows that a twice-done sin becomes 'permitted' to the sinner, so he is stuck in it.

steps.title: Could a sin really become permitted?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is shocked: a sin can't actually become permitted!
steps.simpleTranslation: 'It becomes permitted to him.' Can you really think that?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of רב's statement. A sin can never become halachically allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken literally, 'הותרה לו' would mean the איסור went away, which is impossible. The גמרא pushes back so the words can be explained properly.

keyTerms.meaning: could it enter your mind? (a rhetorical challenge)

phrases.english: It becomes permitted to him — can that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal wording of רב's statement
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'הותרה לו' in רב's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Torah prohibition cannot become permitted because someone repeated the sin.

steps.title: It only feels permitted to him
steps.stepSummary: Correction: the sin becomes to him like something permitted, meaning it feels allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it becomes to him like something permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording. The sin is still forbidden, but in the sinner's mind it now feels allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The change is psychological, not halachic. Because he no longer feels the sin is wrong, he does not feel a need to repent.

keyTerms.meaning: it becomes to him like something permitted

steps.whatToRemember: Repeating a sin does not make it allowed, but it makes it feel allowed. That is why it becomes so hard to stop.

phrases.english: Rather: it becomes to him like something permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by changing the wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewording (אלא): the statement is about perception, not halacha
steps.terutzMaskana: The sin only feels permitted to the sinner

steps.title: Does the משנה go against רבי?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says יום הכפורים does not atone for someone who relies on it. The גמרא suggests this disagrees with רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If one says, I will sin and יום הכפורים will atone, יום הכפורים does not atone.' Shall we say the משנה does not follow רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. It proposes that this line conflicts with the opinion of רבי, and the source for רבי's view comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה limits the power of יום הכפורים when a person relies on it. The גמרא suspects that רבי holds יום הכפורים atones no matter what, which would clash with the משנה.

phrases.english: I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone —
Yom Kippur does not atone.
Shall we say the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that יום הכפורים does not atone for one who relies on it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי holds יום הכפורים atones even without תשובה, the משנה seems to disagree with him.

steps.title: רבי: יום הכפורים atones even without תשובה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי: יום הכפורים atones for all sins, whether or not the person did תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי says, for all the sins in the Torah, whether he repented or did not repent, יום הכפורים atones!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source showing רבי's opinion. This is the support for the suggestion in step 18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי, the day itself brings atonement even without תשובה. That seems to contradict the משנה, which says יום הכפורים does not atone for this person.

keyTerms.meaning: as was taught in a ברייתא

keyTerms.term: בֵּין עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בֵּין לֹא עָשָׂה

phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi says:
For all the sins in the Torah,
whether he repented
or did not repent —
Yom Kippur atones!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source behind the challenge in step 18
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה conflicts with רבי
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא: רבי holds יום הכפורים atones even without תשובה

steps.title: Relying on יום הכפורים is different, even for רבי
steps.stepSummary: The משנה can follow רבי. When someone sins because he is counting on יום הכפורים, even רבי agrees it does not atone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if you say the משנה follows רבי, sinning on the basis of יום הכפורים is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is no contradiction. רבי was talking about ordinary sins, not sins done because the person relies on יום הכפורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי holds that יום הכפורים atones even without תשובה. But a person who uses יום הכפורים as his excuse to sin is a special case, and even רבי agrees the day does not atone for him. The general category of יום הכפורים atoning stays in place; this is only an exception.

keyTerms.meaning: on the basis of, because of

steps.whatToRemember: Even רבי, who holds that יום הכפורים atones without תשובה, agrees that it does not atone for someone who sinned because he relied on it.

phrases.english: Even if you say it follows Rabbi,
"on the basis of" is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 18 and 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception case: רבי agrees in this specific situation
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה can follow רבי, because sinning while relying on יום הכפורים is an exception even for him

steps.title: Quoting the משנה on sins against God
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about sins between a person and God. This opens a new discussion.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Sins between a person and God, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a new line from the משנה. This is a setup for a question about that line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full משנה says that יום הכפורים atones for sins between a person and God. It does not atone for sins between a person and his friend until he appeases his friend. The 'וכו׳' (etc.) points us to that second half, which the גמרא is about to question.

keyTerms.meaning: Between a person and God (מקום is a name for God)
Etc.; the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: Sins that are between a person and God, etc.
phrases.notes: A quote of the משנה, used as a heading for the new discussion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the topic of relying on יום הכפורים to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יום הכפורים atones for sins against God, but not for sins against a friend until the friend is appeased.

steps.title: A verse suggests God forgives sins against people
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חבו points out a contradiction. The פסוק 'אם יחטא איש לאיש ופללו אלהים' seems to say God forgives a person who sins against his friend.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר חבו raised a contradiction to רבי אבהו: Does יום הכפורים really not atone for sins between a person and his friend? But it is written, 'If a man sins against a man, אלהים will ופללו (pray for, forgive) him'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף בר חבו challenges the משנה with a פסוק from שמואל, raising it before רבי אבהו. The פסוק seems to say that God takes care of sins one person does to another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ופללו comes from the root פלל, which can mean prayer. Read that way, the פסוק says God forgives the sinner if he prays. That would mean interpersonal sins can be atoned without appeasing the victim, which goes against the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: He threw at him; he raised a contradiction
Between a person and his friend (interpersonal)
From the root פלל: can mean prayer, forgiveness, or judgment
But it is written! (introduces a verse as a challenge)

phrases.aramaic: רָמֵי לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָבוּ לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Chavu raised a contradiction to Rabbi Abbahu:
Sins that are between a person and his friend
Yom Kippur does not atone for them?
But it is written:
"If a man sins against a man,
phrases.notes: שמואל א ב:כה

phrases.english: God will pray for / forgive him"!
phrases.notes: This assumes אלהים means God and פלל means prayer or forgiveness.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָמֵי לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָבוּ לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the משנה line quoted in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that יום הכפורים does not atone for interpersonal sins.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק seems to say God forgives a sin against another person. So appeasing the victim should not be needed.

steps.title: The word אלהים here means a judge
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו answers that אלהים in this פסוק means a human judge, not God. The פסוק is about a court judging the case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is 'אלהים'? A judge.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers by reading the word אלהים as 'judge' and ופללו as 'will judge him.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אלהים means a בית דין, the פסוק is not talking about God forgiving at all. It says a court will judge the case between the two people. So it does not contradict the משנה.
steps.confusionAlert: In the Torah, אלהים sometimes means human judges, for example in the laws of the שומר. This answer uses that known meaning. It is not saying the word never means God.

phrases.english: Who is 'Elohim'? A judge.
phrases.notes: Read this way, ופללו means 'will judge him.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק says God forgives interpersonal sins.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק says a human judge judges the case. It says nothing about God's forgiveness.

steps.title: The second half of the verse doesn't fit that reading
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חבו pushes back. If פלל means judging, the end of the פסוק would say that no one judges a person who sins against God. That makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, say the end of the verse: 'But if a man sins against God, who will יתפלל for him?'!
steps.whatsHappening: The challenger uses the second half of the same פסוק to attack רבי אבהו's reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two halves of the פסוק use the same root פלל. If it means 'judge' in the first half, the second half would mean 'who will judge him?' That is clearly wrong, since God certainly judges those who sin against Him. So the 'judge' reading seems to fail.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the end part (of the verse)

phrases.english: If so, say the end of the verse:
"But if a man sins against God,
who will intercede (judge?) for him"!
phrases.notes: With the 'judge' reading, this would mean no one judges him, which is impossible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's reading of פלל as 'judging.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same root must mean the same thing in both halves of the פסוק. 'Judge' gives an absurd meaning in the second half.

steps.title: The verse is about forgiveness, not judgment
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו explains the פסוק again, with פלל meaning forgiveness or intercession. For a sin against a person, once the victim is appeased, he will be forgiven. For a sin against God, תשובה and good deeds plead for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the verse means: 'If a man sins against a man, אלהים will ופללו him': he will forgive him. 'But if a man sins against God, who will intercede for him?': תשובה and good deeds.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives a new reading in which both halves of the פסוק make sense. פלל means forgiveness or pleading, not judgment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first half, forgiveness comes once the sinner has made peace with the person he hurt, so it fits the משנה. In the second half, the question 'who will plead for him?' gets an answer: his own תשובה and good deeds. Now the פסוק matches the משנה and both halves read smoothly.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is saying (introduces a re-reading)

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק does not say God forgives sins against people without the victim. Forgiveness for those sins comes after the victim is appeased. For sins against God, תשובה and good deeds plead for the sinner.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
"If a man sins against a man,
Elohim ufilelo him": He will forgive him.
phrases.notes: This happens once the victim has been appeased.

phrases.english: "But if a man sins against God,
who will intercede on his behalf?"
Repentance and good deeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24 by replacing the 'judge' reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new reading of the verse that fits both halves
steps.terutzHavaAmina: פלל means judging, which makes the end of the פסוק absurd.
steps.terutzMaskana: פלל means forgiveness or intercession. Interpersonal sins are forgiven after appeasing the victim, and sins against God through תשובה and good deeds.

steps.title: You must appease someone you hurt, even with words
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that anyone who upsets his friend, even only with words, must appease him. He brings a פסוק from משלי as the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: Anyone who upsets his friend, even just with words, must appease him. As it says: 'My son, if you became a guarantor for your friend, if you shook hands for a stranger, you are trapped by the words of your mouth. Do this then, my son, and save yourself, since you came into your friend's hand: go, humble yourself, and urge your friend.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a practical teaching: hurting someone with words also needs פיוס (appeasement), not only money damage. The proof comes from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק mentions being 'trapped by the words of your mouth.' That shows that words alone can put you 'in your friend's hand.' The פסוק's command, 'go, humble yourself and urge your friend,' is the source for having to go and appease him.

keyTerms.meaning: To appease him; to ask his forgiveness

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the הלכה that before יום הכפורים one must ask forgiveness even for hurtful words.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Anyone who upsets his friend,
even with words, must appease him,
as it is stated:
"My son, if you became a guarantor for your friend,
phrases.notes: משלי ו:א-ג

phrases.english: if you shook hands for a stranger,
you are trapped by the words of your mouth.
phrases.notes: This shows that words alone can create a debt to your friend.

phrases.english: Do this then, my son, and save yourself,
since you have come into your friend's hand:
go, humble yourself, and urge your friend."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: כׇּל הַמַּקְנִיט אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the משנה's demand to appease the victim. It teaches that this applies even to verbal hurt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone who hurts his friend, even only with words, must appease him.

steps.title: How to appease: pay money, or send many friends
steps.stepSummary: The end of the פסוק is explained as two ways to appease. If you owe money, open your hand and pay. If not, send many friends to ask him for forgiveness.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you have money of his in your hand, open your palm to him (pay him). If not, send many friends to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the words of the פסוק. It shows how they teach two kinds of appeasement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word התרפס is read as הַתֵּר פִּסַּת יָד, 'open the palm of the hand,' which means pay what you owe. The word רהב is read as הַרְבֵּה, 'make many,' which means bring many friends to plead with him. Verbal hurt is fixed by the second method.

keyTerms.meaning: Open the palm of the hand (a wordplay on הִתְרַפֵּס)

phrases.english: If you have money (of his) in your hand,
open the palm of your hand to him (pay him),
phrases.notes: This is a play on the word הִתְרַפֵּס in the פסוק.

phrases.english: and if not, send many friends to him.
phrases.notes: This is a play on the word רְהַב. Many people come to ask forgiveness for you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק in step 26 teaches the methods of appeasement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money owed is fixed by paying it. Verbal hurt is fixed by sending many people to ask forgiveness.

steps.title: Appease him with three rows of three people
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא adds that appeasement should be done with three rows of three people. He learns it from the פסוק 'ישור על אנשים' in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: He must appease him with three rows of three people. As it says: 'He comes (ישור) before people and says: I have sinned, and I made crooked what was straight, and it was not worth it for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא adds a detail about how to appease. You should bring three rows, made up of three people, when asking forgiveness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ישור is read like שורה, a row of people. The פסוק describes the confession in three phrases: 'I sinned,' 'I made crooked,' and 'it was not worth it.' This hints at three rows. This adds to רבי יצחק's 'many friends' by giving a set number.

keyTerms.meaning: He comes / looks (read here as related to שׁוּרָה, a row)
I made crooked; I did wrong

steps.whatToRemember: Hurting someone, even with words, needs real appeasement. This can mean asking forgiveness through several groups of people. יום הכפורים alone does not wipe away sins against people.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the halachic practice of asking forgiveness in the presence of others, more than once if needed.

phrases.english: (And) Rav Chisda said:
And he must appease him with three rows
of three people,
as it is stated:
"He comes (in a row) before people
phrases.notes: איוב לג:כז. ישור is read like שורה, a row.

phrases.english: and says: I have sinned, and I made crooked what was straight,
and it was not worth it for me."
phrases.notes: Three phrases of confession hint at three rows.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: וְצָרִיךְ לְפַיְּיסוֹ בְּשָׁלֹשׁ שׁוּרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a set number to רבי יצחק's 'send many friends.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Appeasement should be done with three rows of three people.

steps.title: Do not ask forgiveness more than three times
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא teaches that a person asking forgiveness should not ask more than three times. He learns this from the brothers' request to יוסף.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: Anyone asking forgiveness from his friend should not ask him more than three times. The פסוק says: 'Please, forgive please, and now forgive please.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching sets a limit on how many times you have to ask someone to forgive you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק from when the brothers asked יוסף for forgiveness uses the word 'נא' (please) three times. So three requests are enough. After that the burden moves to the hurt person, who should forgive.

keyTerms.meaning: Forgiveness; asking someone to pardon you

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean you are forbidden to try a fourth time. It means you are not required to keep going after three honest tries.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
Anyone who asks forgiveness from his friend

phrases.aramaic: אַל יְבַקֵּשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ יוֹתֵר מִשָּׁלֹשׁ פְּעָמִים,
phrases.english: should not ask him more than three times,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אָנָּא שָׂא נָא וְעַתָּה שָׂא נָא״.
phrases.english: as it says: 'Please, forgive please, and now forgive please.'
phrases.notes: בראשית נ:יז. 'נא' appears three times.

steps.triggerLanguage: (וְאָמַר) רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא: כׇּל הַמְבַקֵּשׁ מָטוּ מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the laws of appeasing a friend by adding a limit on how many times to ask.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You do not need to ask forgiveness more than three times. This is learned from the three times 'נא' appears in בראשית נ:יז.

steps.title: If the hurt person has died, confess at his grave
steps.stepSummary: If the person you hurt has died, you bring ten people to his grave and confess that you sinned against God and against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he died, he brings ten people and stands them at his grave. He says: 'I sinned against ה׳, the God of Israel, and against so-and-so whom I hurt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The same teaching continues and covers a case where you can no longer ask the person directly because he has died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Death does not cancel the obligation to fix the hurt. You confess in front of ten people, which makes it a public admission. You name both sins: the one against God and the one against the person.

keyTerms.meaning: I hurt or wounded (here, by words or actions)

steps.whatToRemember: Ask forgiveness up to three times. If the person has died, confess at his grave in front of ten people.

phrases.english: And if he died —
he brings ten people
and stands them at his grave, and says:
I have sinned against ה׳, the God of Israel,
and against so-and-so whom I hurt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same speaker continues with the case where the hurt person is no longer alive.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the hurt person has died, you confess at his grave before ten people, naming both your sin against God and your sin against him.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה waits at רבי אבא's door and gets splashed
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא had a complaint against רבי ירמיה. רבי ירמיה went to sit at his door to appease him. A maid's dirty water landed on his head, and he quoted a פסוק about himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא had a complaint against רבי ירמיה. רבי ירמיה went and sat at רבי אבא's doorway. When the maid poured out water, drops landed on his head. He said: 'They made me like a garbage heap.' He applied a פסוק to himself: 'From the garbage heaps He raises up the poor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story showing a חכם humbling himself to ask forgiveness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ירמיה is the one who has to apologize, so he goes to רבי אבא's house and waits humbly. When dirty water falls on him, he does not get angry. He reads it as a sign that God lifts up the lowly.

keyTerms.meaning: He applied a פסוק to himself

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'רבי ירמיה הוה ליה מילתא לרבי אבא בהדיה' mean רבי אבא had the complaint against רבי ירמיה. That is why רבי ירמיה is the one going to apologize.

phrases.english: Concerning Rabbi Yirmeya, there was a grievance
that Rabbi Abba had against him.
He went and sat at the doorway of Rabbi Abba.
While his maid was pouring out water,
drops of the water reached his head.
He said: They have made me like a garbage heap.
He applied a verse to himself: 'From the garbage heaps He raises up the poor.'
phrases.notes: תהלים קיג:ז

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה הֲוָה לֵיהּ מִילְּתָא לְרַבִּי אַבָּא בַּהֲדֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from rules about appeasing to stories that show them in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The person who caused the hurt goes to the other person and humbly waits at his door.

steps.title: רבי אבא goes out to appease רבי ירמיה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא hears what happened and goes out to greet רבי ירמיה. Now רבי אבא feels he must appease רבי ירמיה, and he quotes a פסוק from משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא heard and went out to greet him. He said to him: 'Now I need to appease you, as it is written: Go, humble yourself and urge your friend.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with a twist. The person who was originally hurt now becomes the one who apologizes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because of רבי אבא's household, רבי ירמיה was splashed and embarrassed. So now רבי אבא owes him an apology. He uses the same פסוק that רבי יצחק used earlier as the source for appeasing a friend.

keyTerms.meaning: To appease you (literally, 'to go out onto your mind')

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that hurt can go both ways. Even the person who was wronged must apologize if he later causes hurt.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba heard and went out to greet him.
He said to him: Now I need
to appease you,
as it is written: 'Go, humble yourself and urge your friend.'
phrases.notes: משלי ו:ג, the same פסוק used by רבי יצחק in step 26.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the רבי ירמיה story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If you cause someone embarrassment, even by accident through your household, you must appease him.

steps.title: רבי זירא makes it easy for people to apologize
steps.stepSummary: When רבי זירא had a complaint against someone, he would walk back and forth in front of that person. This made it easy for him to come and apologize.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי זירא had a complaint against someone, he would pass back and forth in front of him and make himself available. That way the person would come and appease him.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story shows how the hurt person can help the other person make peace.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא did not wait for the offender to come find him. He put himself in the person's path so the apology would be easy. The hurt person also has a role in making peace.

phrases.english: When Rabbi Zeira had
a complaint against a person,
he would pass back and forth in front of him
and make himself available to him,
so that he would come
and appease him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא כִּי הֲוָה לֵיהּ מִילְּתָא בַּהֲדֵי אִינִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another story about appeasement. This one is told from the side of the hurt person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The hurt person should make himself available so that the offender can easily apologize.

steps.title: רב goes to appease the butcher, and רב הונא warns of danger
steps.stepSummary: A butcher wronged רב and never came to apologize. On ערב יום כיפור, רב decides to go to him himself. רב הונא predicts that רב is going to 'kill a person.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב had a complaint against a certain butcher, and the butcher did not come to him. On ערב יום כיפור, רב said: 'I will go appease him.' רב הונא met him and asked: 'Where is my master going?' He answered: 'To appease so-and-so.' רב הונא said: 'אבא is going to kill a person.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a third story. רב goes beyond what is required and goes himself to the person who hurt him, and רב הונא gives a dark warning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the butcher was the one who did wrong, רב goes to him to make peace before יום כיפור. רב הונא understands that if the butcher refuses רב's great humility, he will be punished. That is why he says רב is going to 'kill' him. This step builds the tension that the next step resolves.

keyTerms.meaning: ערב יום כיפור, the day before יום כיפור

steps.confusionAlert: 'אבא' here is רב's own name (רב's name was אבא אריכא). It does not mean 'father.'

phrases.english: Rav had a complaint
against a certain butcher,
and the butcher did not come before him.
On the eve of Yom Kippur

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר אִיהוּ: אֵיזִיל אֲנָא לְפַיּוֹסֵי לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: he said: I will go and appease him.
Rav Huna met him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְהֵיכָא קָא אָזֵיל מָר,
phrases.english: He said to him: Where is my master going?
He said to him: To appease so-and-so.
He said: Abba is going to kill a person.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הֲוָה לֵיהּ מִילְּתָא בַּהֲדֵי הָהוּא טַבָּחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes one step further than רבי זירא. רב does not just make himself available; he actually goes to the person who wronged him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before יום כיפור, a great person may even go himself to the one who wronged him to make peace.

steps.title: The butcher refuses and is killed
steps.stepSummary: The butcher sees רב and rudely sends him away. While he is splitting an animal's head, a bone flies out, hits him in the throat, and kills him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב went and stood near him. The butcher was sitting and splitting an animal's head. He raised his eyes and saw him, and said: 'Are you אבא? Go, I have nothing to do with you.' While he was splitting the head, a bone flew out, struck him in the throat, and killed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends, and רב הונא's warning comes true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב humbled himself and came to make peace, but the butcher insulted him and refused. Rejecting such a sincere attempt at peace on ערב יום כיפור brought a severe punishment right away. The story shows how serious it is to refuse an apology.
steps.whatToRemember: Asking forgiveness has limits and rules: three times, and confession at the grave if the person has died. The stories teach humility from both sides. The offender should humble himself, the hurt person should make it easy to apologize, and refusing a sincere apology is extremely dangerous.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story is often cited about the seriousness of making peace before יום כיפור, and about the danger of refusing to forgive.

phrases.english: He went and stood over him.
The butcher was sitting and splitting a head.
He raised his eyes and saw him,
and said to him: Are you Abba?
Go, I have nothing to say to you.
While he was splitting the head,
a bone flew loose
and struck him in his throat and killed him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the רב and butcher story and fulfills רב הונא's prediction.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Refusing a sincere, humble attempt at peace, especially before יום כיפור, can bring a severe punishment.

steps.title: רב reads the Torah portion before רבי, and someone enters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new story: רב was reading the Torah portion in front of רבי. Then someone entered. This passage ends before we learn who it was.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב was reading the Torah portion in front of רבי. Someone came in...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting the scene for a new story about רב. It tells us where רב was and what he was doing, and it starts the next event, someone walking in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story is moving from the butcher to a new scene about רב. The opening line gives the setting: רב is reading the Torah portion in front of his great teacher רבי. The word עֲיַיל ('entered') begins the next event, and the person who entered is named in the continuing text.

keyTerms.meaning: Reading or reciting the Torah portion (verse by verse)
In front of him / before him
רבי יהודה הנשיא, the compiler of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: 'רַבִּי' with no name after it always means רבי יהודה הנשיא. It does not mean just any rabbi.

phrases.english: Rav was reciting the Torah portion
before Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi).
phrases.notes: Sets the scene: the student is reading in front of the teacher.

phrases.english: Entered...
phrases.notes: The sentence is cut off here. The next passage names who entered.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הֲוָה פָּסֵיק סִידְרָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the butcher story ends in step 35, the גמרא begins another story about רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This is the opening scene of a story: רב reading before רבי, and someone entering.
